questions.stem: This upright chest radiograph shows blunting of the costophrenic angle with a meniscus at the lung base. What is the underlying reason fluid produces this blunting at the costophrenic angle first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcified pleural plaques accumulate at the lung base

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluid settles in the most gravity-dependent part of the pleural space

choices.label: C
choices.text: The heart border shifts laterally and covers the angle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Air preferentially rises to the lung apex, sparing the base

choices.label: E
choices.text: Consolidated lung tissue retracts the diaphragm downward

explanation.summary: On an upright film, free pleural fluid layers in the most dependent region, the posterior and lateral costophrenic recesses, blunting the normally sharp angle and forming a meniscus. Several hundred milliliters are usually needed before this sign appears; smaller effusions may only be visible on lateral or decubitus views.
explanation.whyCorrect: On an upright film, free pleural fluid layers in the most dependent region, the posterior and lateral costophrenic recesses, blunting the normally sharp angle and forming a meniscus. Several hundred milliliters are usually needed before this sign appears; smaller effusions may only be visible on lateral or decubitus views.

questions.stem: This normal chest radiograph highlights sharp, well-defined costophrenic angles at both lung bases. What does a sharp costophrenic angle indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Early consolidation of the lower lobe

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevation of the hemidiaphragm from phrenic nerve palsy

choices.label: C
choices.text: A normal, fluid-free pleural space at the lung base

choices.label: D
choices.text: A small pneumothorax at the lung base

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fibrotic scarring of the visceral pleura

explanation.summary: The costophrenic angle is where the diaphragm meets the chest wall. When the pleural space is normal and air-filled lung extends fully into the recess, the angle appears sharp and acute. Loss of this sharpness (blunting) is an early radiographic sign of pleural fluid, so a crisp angle argues against effusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The costophrenic angle is where the diaphragm meets the chest wall. When the pleural space is normal and air-filled lung extends fully into the recess, the angle appears sharp and acute. Loss of this sharpness (blunting) is an early radiographic sign of pleural fluid, so a crisp angle argues against effusion.

questions.stem: This chest radiograph shows near-complete homogeneous white-out of one hemithorax with a concave upper (meniscus) border. What does this appearance most likely represent?

explanation.summary: A large volume of pleural fluid produces a homogeneous opacity that obscures the lung and diaphragm, with a characteristic meniscus (concave superior margin) as fluid tracks up the lateral chest wall. Massive effusions can white-out the hemithorax; if under tension they may push the mediastinum away from the affected side.
explanation.whyCorrect: A large volume of pleural fluid produces a homogeneous opacity that obscures the lung and diaphragm, with a characteristic meniscus (concave superior margin) as fluid tracks up the lateral chest wall. Massive effusions can white-out the hemithorax; if under tension they may push the mediastinum away from the affected side.

questions.stem: This case pairs a frontal (PA) and a lateral chest radiograph, with dashed lines marking blunting at the diaphragm/costophrenic recess. Why is the lateral view especially useful when a small pleural effusion is suspected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It reveals the deep posterior costophrenic recess, where small effusions collect

choices.label: B
choices.text: It measures the exact protein content of the pleural fluid

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shows the heart size more accurately than any effusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: It eliminates the need for any dependent-position imaging

choices.label: E
choices.text: It distinguishes transudates from exudates by density

explanation.summary: The posterior costophrenic sulcus is the deepest, most dependent part of the pleural space and is only seen on the lateral projection. Because fluid pools there first, blunting of the posterior sulcus on the lateral film can detect effusions too small to blunt the lateral costophrenic angle on the frontal view; decubitus films add further sensitivity for free-flowing fluid.
explanation.whyCorrect: The posterior costophrenic sulcus is the deepest, most dependent part of the pleural space and is only seen on the lateral projection. Because fluid pools there first, blunting of the posterior sulcus on the lateral film can detect effusions too small to blunt the lateral costophrenic angle on the frontal view; decubitus films add further sensitivity for free-flowing fluid.

questions.stem: Bilateral pleural effusions are shown on these lateral decubitus chest radiographs. What is the primary diagnostic purpose of obtaining a lateral decubitus view in a patient with suspected pleural effusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To quantify the ejection fraction of the heart

choices.label: B
choices.text: To assess for endobronchial tumor obstruction

choices.label: C
choices.text: To evaluate coronary artery calcium burden

choices.label: D
choices.text: To determine whether the effusion is free-flowing or loculated

choices.label: E
choices.text: To measure the diameter of the pulmonary artery

explanation.summary: On a lateral decubitus film, a free-flowing effusion layers dependently along the dependent chest wall, whereas a loculated effusion stays fixed. Demonstrating layering confirms the fluid is mobile and can be safely sampled or drained.
explanation.whyCorrect: On a lateral decubitus film, a free-flowing effusion layers dependently along the dependent chest wall, whereas a loculated effusion stays fixed. Demonstrating layering confirms the fluid is mobile and can be safely sampled or drained.

questions.stem: These paired thoracic ultrasound images contrast a normal scan (top) with an abnormal one (bottom) in which the vertebral bodies remain visible above the diaphragm. What does this 'spine sign' indicate?

explanation.summary: Normally, air in the lung scatters ultrasound so the spine cannot be traced above the diaphragm (spine sign absent). When pleural fluid is present, it transmits sound and allows the vertebral column to be seen above the diaphragm, producing a positive spine sign.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normally, air in the lung scatters ultrasound so the spine cannot be traced above the diaphragm (spine sign absent). When pleural fluid is present, it transmits sound and allows the vertebral column to be seen above the diaphragm, producing a positive spine sign.

questions.stem: This illustration shows a patient sitting upright and leaning forward while a needle drains fluid from the pleural space into a collection bag. What procedure is depicted?

explanation.summary: Thoracentesis is performed with the patient upright and leaning forward so that fluid pools posteriorly and inferiorly; a needle is introduced above a rib into the pleural space to withdraw the effusion for diagnostic analysis or symptomatic relief.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thoracentesis is performed with the patient upright and leaning forward so that fluid pools posteriorly and inferiorly; a needle is introduced above a rib into the pleural space to withdraw the effusion for diagnostic analysis or symptomatic relief.

questions.stem: On the lateral view of this chest radiograph, fluid tracks upward along the chest wall producing an upwardly concave border. What is this radiographic finding called and what does it signify?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Meniscus sign, indicating a free-flowing pleural effusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kerley B lines, indicating interstitial edema

choices.label: D
choices.text: Silhouette sign, indicating right middle lobe collapse

explanation.summary: The meniscus sign is the upwardly concave interface of pleural fluid against the chest wall, caused by surface tension and the fluid tracking higher laterally. It confirms a free-flowing effusion and results in blunting/loss of the costophrenic angles.
explanation.whyCorrect: The meniscus sign is the upwardly concave interface of pleural fluid against the chest wall, caused by surface tension and the fluid tracking higher laterally. It confirms a free-flowing effusion and results in blunting/loss of the costophrenic angles.

questions.stem: On this axial chest CT, the arrow labeled 'dilated bronchi' points to abnormally widened, thick-walled airways in the right lung. What term describes this permanent airway dilation?

explanation.summary: Permanent, abnormal dilation of the bronchi with thickened walls is bronchiectasis, often resulting from chronic infection or inflammation with destruction of the airway wall. Here it accompanies pneumonia and a pleural effusion in the right lung.
explanation.whyCorrect: Permanent, abnormal dilation of the bronchi with thickened walls is bronchiectasis, often resulting from chronic infection or inflammation with destruction of the airway wall. Here it accompanies pneumonia and a pleural effusion in the right lung.

questions.stem: This diagram compares a normal hemithorax with one containing a pleural effusion. Approximately what volume of pleural fluid must accumulate before it becomes clinically/radiographically significant, as contrasted here?

explanation.summary: The normal pleural space contains only a few milliliters of lubricating fluid (<15 mL). Accumulation beyond this small physiologic amount represents a pleural effusion, which compresses the underlying lung.
explanation.whyCorrect: The normal pleural space contains only a few milliliters of lubricating fluid (<15 mL). Accumulation beyond this small physiologic amount represents a pleural effusion, which compresses the underlying lung.

questions.stem: This diagram of a capillary shows four Starling forces (Pc, Pi, πc, πi) governing fluid movement into and out of the pleural/interstitial space. Which force is the principal driver pushing fluid OUT of the capillary?

explanation.summary: Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) is the dominant outward force driving filtration of fluid across the capillary wall. Capillary oncotic pressure (πc) is the main opposing force pulling fluid back in. Imbalance of these Starling forces (e.g., elevated Pc in heart failure or reduced πc in hypoalbuminemia) leads to effusion formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) is the dominant outward force driving filtration of fluid across the capillary wall. Capillary oncotic pressure (πc) is the main opposing force pulling fluid back in. Imbalance of these Starling forces (e.g., elevated Pc in heart failure or reduced πc in hypoalbuminemia) leads to effusion formation.

questions.stem: The crosshairs in this diagram and the accompanying photo mark the standard site for emergency needle decompression by the anterior approach. Which landmark do they indicate?

explanation.summary: The classic anterior approach for needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax targets the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line, passing just above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
explanation.whyCorrect: The classic anterior approach for needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax targets the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line, passing just above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.

questions.stem: This labeled PA chest radiograph is provided as a reference. Compared with a pneumothorax, which feature confirms that this lung is normally expanded?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A sharp visceral pleural line with lucency beyond it

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lung markings (vascular shadows) extend all the way to the chest wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: A collapsed lung crumpled at the hilum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Absence of any lung markings in the periphery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deviation of the trachea to one side

explanation.summary: In a normal lung, peripheral vascular (lung) markings extend to the inner chest wall. In pneumothorax, air in the pleural space produces a visceral pleural line with absent lung markings peripheral to it. This normal film serves as the comparison baseline.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a normal lung, peripheral vascular (lung) markings extend to the inner chest wall. In pneumothorax, air in the pleural space produces a visceral pleural line with absent lung markings peripheral to it. This normal film serves as the comparison baseline.

questions.stem: On this PA chest radiograph, the left upper zone is abnormally lucent with no vascular markings extending to the chest wall. What radiographic feature establishes the diagnosis of pneumothorax?

choices.label: B
choices.text: An air-fluid level with a meniscus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Absence of lung markings peripheral to a visceral pleural line

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased vascular markings throughout the affected lung

explanation.summary: Pneumothorax is diagnosed by a thin visceral pleural line with a lucent, avascular space (air) beyond it, since collapsed lung retracts and no vessels reach the chest wall. This left-sided example shows loss of peripheral lung markings.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pneumothorax is diagnosed by a thin visceral pleural line with a lucent, avascular space (air) beyond it, since collapsed lung retracts and no vessels reach the chest wall. This left-sided example shows loss of peripheral lung markings.

questions.stem: These images show a right-sided non-tension pneumothorax (highlighted). The overlay demonstrates the mediastinum remaining midline. What key feature distinguishes this from a tension pneumothorax?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Presence of an air-fluid level in the pleural space

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contralateral tracheal deviation with mediastinal shift

choices.label: D
choices.text: Absence of mediastinal shift toward the contralateral side

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complete opacification of the affected hemithorax

explanation.summary: In a simple (non-tension) pneumothorax the mediastinum stays midline because intrapleural pressure does not progressively rise. A tension pneumothorax, by contrast, shifts the mediastinum and trachea away from the affected side and compromises venous return, constituting an emergency.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a simple (non-tension) pneumothorax the mediastinum stays midline because intrapleural pressure does not progressively rise. A tension pneumothorax, by contrast, shifts the mediastinum and trachea away from the affected side and compromises venous return, constituting an emergency.

questions.stem: On this chest radiograph, branching lucent streaks outline the fibers of the pectoralis major over the chest wall (the 'ginkgo leaf' appearance). What process produces this pattern?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Air tracking into the subcutaneous soft tissues

explanation.summary: The ginkgo-leaf sign is caused by free gas (subcutaneous emphysema) dissecting between the fibers of the pectoralis major, here associated with a right pneumothorax marked by a visible pleural edge.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ginkgo-leaf sign is caused by free gas (subcutaneous emphysema) dissecting between the fibers of the pectoralis major, here associated with a right pneumothorax marked by a visible pleural edge.

questions.stem: The right (M-mode) panel of this lung ultrasound shows uniform horizontal lines all the way down (a 'barcode' or 'stratosphere' pattern) instead of a granular 'seashore' below the pleural line. What does this indicate?

explanation.summary: Loss of lung sliding abolishes the granular 'seashore' pattern; the resulting uniform horizontal 'barcode/stratosphere' sign in M-mode indicates air in the pleural space (pneumothorax).
explanation.whyCorrect: Loss of lung sliding abolishes the granular 'seashore' pattern; the resulting uniform horizontal 'barcode/stratosphere' sign in M-mode indicates air in the pleural space (pneumothorax).

questions.stem: The photo highlights the 'sentinel hole' (the most proximal side-hole, cut through the tube's radiopaque stripe). Why is it clinically important that this hole lies inside the pleural cavity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If it sits outside the chest wall, air is entrained

choices.label: B
choices.text: It allows the tube to be flushed with saline

choices.label: C
choices.text: It marks the depth to which sutures must be placed

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is where suction pressure is measured

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the only hole that actually drains fluid

explanation.summary: The sentinel side-hole is placed through the radiopaque stripe so its position can be confirmed on X-ray; if it lies outside the pleural space it entrains air, causing an air leak, ongoing pneumothorax, or subcutaneous emphysema.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sentinel side-hole is placed through the radiopaque stripe so its position can be confirmed on X-ray; if it lies outside the pleural space it entrains air, causing an air leak, ongoing pneumothorax, or subcutaneous emphysema.

questions.stem: The curled radiopaque device seen within the hemithorax (a pigtail catheter) is generally preferred over a large-bore chest tube for draining which of the following?

explanation.summary: Small-bore pigtail catheters effectively evacuate air with less pain than large-bore tubes and are well suited to simple pneumothorax; viscous or particulate collections (blood, pus, clot) require a larger-bore chest tube.
explanation.whyCorrect: Small-bore pigtail catheters effectively evacuate air with less pain than large-bore tubes and are well suited to simple pneumothorax; viscous or particulate collections (blood, pus, clot) require a larger-bore chest tube.

questions.stem: What imaging study is shown here?

explanation.summary: This is a standing PA chest radiograph, showing the ribs, lungs, mediastinum, and hemidiaphragms with the characteristic grayscale of plain film.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is a standing PA chest radiograph, showing the ribs, lungs, mediastinum, and hemidiaphragms with the characteristic grayscale of plain film.

questions.stem: The inset shows apical thin-walled air sacs on the lung surface. Rupture of these lesions classically causes primary spontaneous pneumothorax in which patient group?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pregnant women in the third trimester

explanation.summary: Rupture of subpleural apical blebs/bullae causes primary spontaneous pneumothorax, which classically occurs in tall, thin young men without underlying lung disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rupture of subpleural apical blebs/bullae causes primary spontaneous pneumothorax, which classically occurs in tall, thin young men without underlying lung disease.

questions.stem: This thoracoscopic view shows a thin-walled, translucent air-filled blister on the surface of the lung. What is it?

explanation.summary: The pale, thin-walled outpouching on the visceral pleural surface is a bleb/bulla; rupture of such lesions is the usual cause of spontaneous pneumothorax and they are often stapled/resected at VATS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pale, thin-walled outpouching on the visceral pleural surface is a bleb/bulla; rupture of such lesions is the usual cause of spontaneous pneumothorax and they are often stapled/resected at VATS.

questions.stem: This clinical illustration shows distended neck veins, tracheal deviation toward the uninjured side, hyperresonance with absent breath sounds on one side, hypotension, and air hunger. What emergency is depicted?

explanation.summary: Tension pneumothorax occurs when a one-way air leak progressively raises intrapleural pressure, shifting the mediastinum/trachea toward the contralateral side, impeding venous return (distended neck veins, hypotension), and causing hyperresonance with absent breath sounds. It requires immediate needle decompression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tension pneumothorax occurs when a one-way air leak progressively raises intrapleural pressure, shifting the mediastinum/trachea toward the contralateral side, impeding venous return (distended neck veins, hypotension), and causing hyperresonance with absent breath sounds. It requires immediate needle decompression.

questions.stem: In this three-bottle chest drainage setup, what is the function of the middle 'water seal' bottle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It humidifies air returning to the lung

choices.label: B
choices.text: It acts as a one-way valve that lets air out

choices.label: C
choices.text: It regulates the maximum applied suction pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: It measures the volume of the pleural air leak directly

choices.label: E
choices.text: It collects drained fluid from the lung

explanation.summary: The water seal bottle is a one-way valve: air from the pleural space bubbles out through the submerged tube but water prevents atmospheric air from being drawn back in. The pressure-regulating bottle sets suction and the collection bottle traps fluid.
explanation.whyCorrect: The water seal bottle is a one-way valve: air from the pleural space bubbles out through the submerged tube but water prevents atmospheric air from being drawn back in. The pressure-regulating bottle sets suction and the collection bottle traps fluid.

questions.stem: This diagram compares a normal lung with a pneumothorax. When air accumulates in the pleural space, why does the underlying lung collapse?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood displaces air from the alveoli

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lung parenchyma is destroyed by the entering air

choices.label: C
choices.text: The diaphragm actively compresses the lung

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bronchial mucus plugging blocks airflow to the lobe

choices.label: E
choices.text: The air abolishes the negative intrapleural pressure

explanation.summary: The lung is normally held open by negative intrapleural pressure. When air enters the pleural space this negative pressure is lost, the lung's elastic recoil is unopposed, and it collapses inward.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lung is normally held open by negative intrapleural pressure. When air enters the pleural space this negative pressure is lost, the lung's elastic recoil is unopposed, and it collapses inward.

questions.stem: This H&E section shows sheets of polygonal cells with abundant pink cytoplasm and relatively uniform round nuclei arising from the pleura. This is the most common histologic subtype of which malignancy?

explanation.summary: Epithelioid morphology, resembling reactive mesothelial cells, is the most common and most favorable histologic pattern of malignant mesothelioma; immunostains (calretinin, WT-1) confirm mesothelial origin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Epithelioid morphology, resembling reactive mesothelial cells, is the most common and most favorable histologic pattern of malignant mesothelioma; immunostains (calretinin, WT-1) confirm mesothelial origin.

questions.stem: This pleural biopsy shows branching papillary fronds lined by cuboidal cells with fibrovascular cores. Which immunohistochemical marker best supports a mesothelial (rather than adenocarcinoma) origin?

explanation.summary: The papillary epithelioid pattern is characteristic of mesothelioma; calretinin (and WT-1, D2-40) are positive in mesothelioma, whereas TTF-1, CEA, and napsin A favor pulmonary adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The papillary epithelioid pattern is characteristic of mesothelioma; calretinin (and WT-1, D2-40) are positive in mesothelioma, whereas TTF-1, CEA, and napsin A favor pulmonary adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: This coronal chest CT shows circumferential rind-like soft-tissue thickening encasing the pleural surface (arrows/circle) with associated effusion. In a patient with prior asbestos exposure, this is most consistent with which diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Nodular, circumferential pleural thickening that encases the lung with effusion is the classic CT appearance of malignant mesothelioma, strongly associated with asbestos exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nodular, circumferential pleural thickening that encases the lung with effusion is the classic CT appearance of malignant mesothelioma, strongly associated with asbestos exposure.

questions.stem: This lateral chest radiograph highlights a discrete calcified density along the diaphragmatic pleura. What exposure history is most strongly associated with development of this lesion?

explanation.summary: Calcified pleural plaques, especially over the diaphragm and posterolateral chest wall, are a marker of prior asbestos exposure and raise concern for mesothelioma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Calcified pleural plaques, especially over the diaphragm and posterolateral chest wall, are a marker of prior asbestos exposure and raise concern for mesothelioma.

questions.stem: This frontal chest radiograph shows blunting of the costophrenic angle with a meniscus at the right lung base. What is the mechanism producing this radiographic finding in advanced pleural malignancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of fluid in the pleural space

choices.label: B
choices.text: Collapse of alveoli from airway obstruction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Air trapped in the pleural space

explanation.summary: The basal opacity with a meniscus is a pleural effusion; malignant pleural involvement (e.g., mesothelioma) impairs fluid resorption and commonly presents with a unilateral effusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The basal opacity with a meniscus is a pleural effusion; malignant pleural involvement (e.g., mesothelioma) impairs fluid resorption and commonly presents with a unilateral effusion.

questions.stem: This gross specimen of the parietal pleura shows circumscribed, pearly-white, waxy fibrous patches (circled). These lesions are a hallmark of remote exposure to which agent?

explanation.summary: Discrete, ivory-white collagenous plaques on the parietal and diaphragmatic pleura are the classic gross marker of prior asbestos exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Discrete, ivory-white collagenous plaques on the parietal and diaphragmatic pleura are the classic gross marker of prior asbestos exposure.

questions.stem: This cross-sectioned specimen shows a thick, firm, tan-white tumor that circumferentially encases and constricts the underlying lung. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A rind of tumor encasing the entire lung and encroaching on fissures is the characteristic gross appearance of diffuse malignant pleural mesothelioma.
explanation.whyCorrect: A rind of tumor encasing the entire lung and encroaching on fissures is the characteristic gross appearance of diffuse malignant pleural mesothelioma.
